newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco firms said to offer vending, ad concessions.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco firms said to offer vending, ad concessions.

text.p: The tobacco industry would accept a ban on all cigarette vending machines, halt all outdoor advertising and pay hundreds of millions a year for anti-smoking campaigns as part of a package of concessions in exchange for immunity, the Washington Post reported Thursday.

Quoting unidentified sources, the newspaper said talks between the tobacco industry and its adversaries were about to resume over the critical hurdle of how much immunity the industry would get from lawsuits.
Discussions recessed 10 days ago with the immunity issue dividing the two sides.
The Post said a core group of negotiators was scheduled to meet Thursday in Washington to look at options for a middle ground on the immunity question.

The tobacco industry was seeking "blanket immunity" from virtually all lawsuits, while its adversaries, paticularly 24 state attorneys general, say it would be unfair to close off the courts to individuals who believed they had been harmed by smoking, sources familiar with the negotiations told the Post.
Presidential aide Bruce Lindsey met at the White House on Wednesday with all parties in ongoing talks to reach a tobacco settlement, according to officials who declined to discuss the negotiations.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the talks dealt with last week's U.S. district court ruling that the government can regulate tobacco sales and marketing, but not promotion and advertising.
President Clinton has said he will appeal the limits on government regulatory powers imposed by the court.
The White House talks also involved efforts by the 24 state attorneys general who have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs for treating smokers.
